en: Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Oṃ, salutations to Sarasvatī. Oṃ, Subrata, tell me how Sarasvatī is attained and by what means;
speak of how the goddess Mahāsarasvatī becomes pleased.
The venerable Āśvalāyana said:
Listen, all you sages, to this great [teaching], more secret than the secret;
renowned as the "Ten Verses," I shall speak it preceded by meditation.
One should meditate upon the four-armed goddess, who holds a goad and a rosary, and carries a noose and a book, and is enveloped by garlands of flames.
Adorned with a white garment resembling a mirror, she possessed beautiful breasts and a slender waist; she had the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
She was endowed with a mass of matted locks, her face resembling the full moon,
and she was adorned with bracelets rich in gold and jewels, as well as strings of pearls.
The great goddess Trilocanā, wearing golden anklets and illuminating the three worlds with her armlets, girdle, and other ornaments.
One who desires knowledge, being composed in mind, should meditate upon the fire-drill of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
[Oṃ] Of this mantra of the Śrī Sarasvatī-stotra, Āśvalāyana is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ),

the goddess Śrī Vāgvādinī is the deity (devatā), "daivīṃ vācamajamati" is the seed-syllable (bīja), "yadvāk" is the power (śakti), and "praṇodevī" is the pin (kīlaka). [This is employed] for the sake of attaining the grace of the goddess Sarasvatī for oneself, and for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord.
The application in the recitation is as follows: || 9 ||

Oṃ! Having prostrated before the Goddess who is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, the bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, I praise that very Sarasvatī, the power of knowledge. 10.
May that Sarasvatī protect me— she who, in ultimate reality, has as her sole nature the truth taught by the Vedānta, yet is manifested in the form of name and form.
May that Sarasvatī, the non-dual power of Brahman who is praised as one alone throughout the four Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs, protect me. 12.
May that Sarasvatī protect me— she who is proclaimed in the form of the meaning of letters, words, and sentences, and who is without beginning or end and infinite.

May that Sarasvatī, established in the form of Brahman, protect me— she into whom all things, such as name, birth, and so forth, are again dissolved, and whom those abiding in the nature of Brahman meditate upon.
May that Sarasvatī, who is conceived as eightfold through distinctions such as name, genus, and so forth, yet is in truth one and non-conceptual in nature, protect me. 15.
May that Sarasvatī protect me—she who is the pervasive, singular form of pure consciousness, experienced by the wise through their inward vision as she is being manifested. 16.
May that Sarasvatī protect me— she who pervades the universe within by her very nature and enters the three worlds, abiding in the forms of Rudra, Āditya, and the rest.
May that Sarasvatī protect me— she who, as the perfect sovereign of the gods, both internally and with respect to the divine, dwells within as the inner self while speaking.
May that Sarasvatī, the cow who milks all desires, protect me—she whom all the gods and others, both manifest and unmanifest, utter in their speech. (19)
May that Sarasvatī protect me— having known whom, the yogi, having crushed all bondage by means of the stainless path, goes to the supreme abode.
He who desires fearless poetic skill, as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation,
should worship and praise Sarasvatī with devotion by means of these ten verses.
For one devoid of devotion and faith, realization shall arise within six months;
thereafter, speech flows forth at will in graceful syllables.
A poet born of Sarasvatī generally understands a work—whether consisting of prose and verse or containing the intended objects of knowledge—that has not been heard before. (23)
One shall quickly retain what has been heard, one's speech shall become clear and free from stammering;
renowned throughout all worlds, one becomes an eloquent speaker and is honored. || 24 ||
When a dispute arises with those within one's own group or with those outside the Vedic fold, he becomes invincible to his opponents and himself emerges as the victor. (25)
One should contemplate: "I am Vācaspati, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
By contemplating in this way, even Vācaspati himself [is attained]. 26.
He is unable to speak with equanimity even toward other men, let alone others;
he must not revile any woman, nor the gods, nor indeed the twice-born. (27)
One should not utter slander against others, nor should one treat women with contempt; one should not converse with the ignoble and should remain patient in all circumstances. (28)
One should always speak kindly if one desires success for oneself;
one should overcome that hostile opponent with verses alone. (29)
Such a person becomes a lion among the elephants of opposing disputants, for he always worships the Goddess with the very verse beginning with "yadvāk. (30)
From his mouth never issues any speech that is unrefined;
you are the manifest presence of all beings, as well as heaven itself and the stability of the earth.

O supreme Ambikā, who dwells within the womb of the gods, those who call you "Mother," "Durgā," or "Ambikā"— [may they be blessed by] the nourishment of modesty, as well as anger, forgiveness, and contentment.
With bodies bowed in reverence, they will offer praise both in the morning and in the afternoon, saying: "O Blessed One! O Auspicious One! O Peaceful One! O Most Peaceful One! (33)
For by your grace, everything they desire shall come to pass;
you, being worshipped with offerings of milk, curd, and various kinds of foods and edibles, [will grant their wishes].
When she is pleased, she bestows all the desires of men without exception. || 34 ||
She who is as white as a kunda flower, the moon, frost, or a pearl necklace; she who is draped in radiant white garments;
she whose hands are adorned with a lute and the gesture of granting boons; she who sits upon a white lotus throne;
and she who is eternally saluted by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all other gods.
May that blessed Sarasvatī, who removes all dullness without exception, protect me. 35.
Endowed with four arms, she holds a rosary made of crystal;
in one hand she holds a white lotus, and in another, a parrot and a book.
May that Goddess of Speech, who shines with a splendor resembling jasmine, the moon, a conch, and crystal, and who is peerless—may she dwell forever in my mouth, ever well-pleased. (36)
May that Goddess Sarasvatī, who is constantly praised by Brahmā, Indra, the gods, and the kinnaras, and who holds a lotus in her hand, dwell upon the tip of my tongue.
May Vāṇī, who holds a noose and a goad, and who bears a lute and a book—pure as milk, a kunda flower, and the moon—dwell eternally within my mouth. (38)
Thus Āśvalāyana has proclaimed this hymn of the Goddess, which serves as a repository for the enjoyment of identical words;
the best of the twice-born who recites this attains purity.
It immediately and swiftly brings about the fruits of one's well-wished desires. || 39 ||
Thus ends the Śrī Sarasvatī Stotra composed by the venerable great sage Āśvalāyana.
May there be auspiciousness for all living beings.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady Śārikā.
Oṃ, since the act of salutation, the object of salutation, and the one who salutes are not separate, I thus salute myself;
indeed, I am eternally [saluted] by my own self. (1)
This commentary on the Mantras has been composed by the son of Somānanda, a resident of Vijayeśvara, using well-determined words and sentences. (2)
From the initiation ceremony onwards, one should be a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī). || 1 ||

The *upanayana* is the bringing of the disciple’s mind—which is of the nature of Brahman—into proximity with the Guru as its agent; it is the joining of one's own mind [with that of the disciple]. As was previously stated: "I give my heart to your vow; let your mind be in accordance with my mind," and so forth. From that time onward, the practitioner of vows is a *brahmacārin*.

The attainment of proximity to the Guru who is the very nature of Brahman, and abiding in the form of the Guru—this is the primary vow (*vrata*), meaning conduct, behavior, or state of being. Furthermore, *upanayana* (initiation) is the attainment of proximity to the Guru who is the very nature of Brahman;
that is to say, the attainment of non-difference from Him. From that point onward, the vows to be described hereafter constitute the practice (*carita*) and the manifestation (*saṃbhava*).
"Not otherwise" (*nānyathā*): the suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). [This concludes] the second section on dwelling on the path.
On the path—that is, on the pure way—one should dwell as one with Brahman, characterized by that [state]; this is to be understood as applying everywhere. || 2 ||
With hair gathered together. || 3 ||
The sense objects, such as the female organ (*bhaga*) and so forth, are capable of bestowing perishable pleasure;

however, for him who has uprooted the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that had arisen toward the flavors of those sense objects, they have become destructive—this is the meaning. Alternatively, "ka" means happiness, which is like a drop (*bindu*) arising from the enjoyment of sense objects.

His Lord—the cause that is the Master—is Brahmānanda in the form of the ocean; he is one whose [nature] is compact, joined with firm joints, and who has not entered the path of ordinary experience—such is the Creator (Vidhi). The meaning is that he is a mass of consciousness and bliss (cidānandaghana). Precisely because the attainment of consciousness and bliss necessarily follows immediately after the purification of the path (adhvan), [this is stated].

Having said "dwelling on the path," he says "with hair bound together. According to Amara, "saṃhata" means one whose joints are firm. He instructs her to worship that [deity] in order to perform the subduing of the body and so forth, which will be described hereafter. (3)
His livelihood shall consist of wandering for alms. || 4 ||

"Bhaikṣya" refers to repeatedly requesting instruction on the reality (tattva) from teachers who provide explanations of mantras such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi). He whose livelihood or wages consist of this—he is one whose mind is constantly intent upon hearing the statements of Vedānta; such is the meaning. || 4 ||
The *saśalka* and *vaṃdu* [trees] are [to be used]. || 5 ||
He who possesses a staff for subduing [the senses] everywhere— whether it be the bark-covered skin or the body itself— or rather,

he who has become free from attachment by abandoning the conceit of self in what is not-self; or else, he whose non-subduing of the "scales"— meaning the body, speech, and mind, which are the life-breaths clinging to the body— is [controlled], such a one is a *tridaṇḍin*.
This is the meaning. And it has been said:
"The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body—he whose restraints are fixed in these three is called a *tridaṇḍin*."

The letter *ka* denotes the wind (*vāyu*). Through the subduing of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone, there is the restraint of the mind (*manas*). For the mind and the vital breath are eternally associated, due to their constant coexistence. || 5 ||
He should wear a girdle made of seven strands of muñja grass.
The word "Buddhi" is to be understood as the subject. Regarding the verbal root *muji*: there are seven in number.
These are the *muñjas*, which are the *vimarśas* (reflections), corresponding to the stages (*bhūmikās*) of the desire for purity (*śubhecchā*). These are well-known in the Yoga Śāstra:
"The first stage of knowledge is proclaimed by the name Śubhecchā."
Vicāraṇā is the second, and Tanumānasā is the third.
The fourth is the attainment of existence (sattāpatti); after that is the one named attachment (saṃsakti).
The sixth is the meditation on the categories of reality (padārthabhāvanā), and the seventh is remembered as the state beyond the four (turyagā).
Thus are those belonging to the formless realm.
In that regard, the first stage for those seeking liberation consists of the discernment of the eternal and the non-eternal, and so forth, culminating in the final fruit.
Then, having approached a guru, the investigation of the Vedānta texts, consisting of hearing and reflection, constitutes the second [stage]. || 2 ||
Then, through the practice of placing [the mind] and one-pointedness of consciousness, there arises a third [stage]: fitness for the investigation of extremely subtle objects. III.3.
Beyond that, the fourth stage is indeed the direct cause arising from Paramaśiva.

This alone is the nature of the fruit. The other three, beginning with non-attachment, are merely its specific manifestations. Among the first three, there is the state of waking because of the manifestation of duality and its differentiation. The fourth, however, is the state of dreaming because of the manifestation of the world's falsity. || 4 ||
The state of non-conceptual meditative absorption is characterized by non-attachment; it is deep sleep. || 5 ||

Therefore, the yogin emerges from that state by himself. Then, through the maturation of that practice, there arises a profound sleep characterized by the manifestation of objects, which persists for a long duration.
Therefore, emergence occurs through the effort of another. || 6 ||

That state in which one does not emerge from it either by oneself or through another— because the appearance of duality no longer manifests at all— but rather remains everywhere and at all times as the Supreme Lord himself, a solid mass of perfect supreme bliss; that is the seventh state, the *turya* (the Fourth).

This very [intellect], in the form of a girdle (*mekhalā*), possessing reflective awareness (*vimarśavatī*) through the seven stages beginning with *śubhecchā*, "takes" (*lāti*)—that is, grasps—the "Me," which is the void (*kham*), the body of space, namely Brahman. One should maintain such an intellect through the experience of awakening to subtle reality; the meaning is that one becomes pure Brahman. Thus...
He states that for one who has attained pure union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*), the renunciation of wealth, wife, and so forth will necessarily come about. || 6 ||
"Not honey or meat," and so forth: "One should not eat honey or meat. (7)

The accumulation of wealth is like honey collected by bees; the body is a loathsome thing, consisting of flesh and blood. You should not consume either of these; abandon attachment to them. As it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭhayoga*:
"The ignorant do not long for riches, just as they do not long for darkness. Likewise:

"Where are the flesh, blood, and so forth, and where are you, whose very form is consciousness? However, some [hold that] the entire body, distinct from the individual soul (jīva), is flesh; [the text says] "in the body of flesh," [referring to] the male form, which one tastes like honey.

"You should not eat; rather, you should consume whatever comes to you, remaining entirely unattached and having abandoned the notion of taste, solely by the force of the impressions (saṃskāra) of your past actions," so they said. || 7 ||
They should avoid alkaline substances and salt. || 8 ||

The states of being of the heroine Sragvandanā are indestructible by salt; her "saltiness" (lavaṇa), due to the predominance of her essential nature, excludes mere physical beauty (lāvaṇya). Such is her character. || 1 ||
The meaning is that they are devoid of flavor due to the cultivation of the perception of worthlessness in worldly objects. || 8 ||
One who is not hostile toward the teacher. || 9 ||
The teacher’s single-minded devotion to Brahman is equal to the abandonment of all that is contrary to the state of being synonymous with the ultimate reality. || 9 ||
He is independent in all his actions. || 10 ||
Through the knowledge that all actions and desired goals are dependent upon Īśvara, one’s mind becomes free from the sense of "I."
One who rises early. || 11 ||
In the previous case, the notion that superimposition is possible between the eye and the cloth is logical. || 11 ||
He should sleep at the last. || 12 ||
Regarding a subsequent action that occurs later, [the thought] "it does not exist" arises; this is a dream due to non-attachment to conditions. 12.
Whatever may come to you, that you should give to us. || 13 ||
Whatever one might resort to as the self—whether it be conceived through conceptual construction as gross or subtle—[it is not the true self].

Then you should offer [yourself] to the Preceptor, the Lord who impels all; by that Lord whose mind is impelled, you should dissolve all that is conceptualized within the state of inward-turned awareness.
He with whom one is connected among many should give that to us. || 14 ||

Among the various imagined states of existence, you have become immersed in those specific conceptualizations by means of whichever imagined object is appropriate for you. All of that belongs to this [Self]. It arises as the Self, which is the object of all experience, through the thought "I am. Seek it; therefore, it has come. By this, the state of being established is indicated.
You should lead all this toward that state.
There is no distinction regarding his bed. || 15 ||

Do not enter this bed of forgetfulness, which is another name for the dissolution (*laya*) of this self; with your mind entered [into the Self], may you become awakened. As it is said from the perspective of the Vedāntins: "One should awaken the mind during dissolution, and again pacify it when it is distracted."
He teaches while cultivating [the state]. || 15 ||
Mount the man and the chariot. || 16 ||
Nor should you mount the chariot whose form is the mind with excessive speed; the meaning is that you should be one who has abandoned all volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*).

Alternatively, "do not mount the chariot" means do not mount the body. For mounting the body consists in the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) characterized by the cognition of that which is not the Self—such as the body and senses—as being the Self; [therefore,] you, the inner Self, [should remain as such]. O son...

Regarding the superimposition of external attributes (*bāhyadharmādhyāsa*), there is the thought: "Among the various options regarding what is called 'wife,' I alone am the one who is either deficient or complete.

Likewise, there is the superimposition of bodily attributes (*dehadharmādhyāsa*), such as: "I am thin," "I am stout," "I stand," or "I walk. Similarly, there is the superimposition of sensory attributes (*indriyadharmādhyāsa*), such as: "I am mute," "I am one-eyed," "I am impotent," or "I am deaf. Likewise, [there is the thought]: "I am happy..."
The meaning is: "I am suffering"—you should abandon this superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

You should know that there is only a mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) between the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and the not-self (*anātman*), which are absolutely distinct and of contradictory natures like darkness and light, as well as between their respective attributes. [Know] the Self...
"Know the body to be the chariot and the self to be the charioteer," according to the Śruti; thus, the Shaiva scripture states that the coverings such as Māyā are like garments for the soul. || 16 ||
You should not clothe yourself. || 17 ||

Just as illusion (*māyā*) and the like do not constitute a covering in the manner of a garment, so you should act; the meaning is that you must abandon the wrapping of the three sheaths (*kośatraya*). And the three sheaths have been described as follows: "In this context, the supreme covering is impurity (*mala*);
the subtle is the casing of *māyā* and the rest; and the gross is the external form of the body—this is the triad of sheaths."

For the self is indeed enveloped; due to its connection with the darkness of ignorance, it perceives even its own single nature as the self through the manifold diversity of the grasped and the grasper. || 17 ||
One should avoid all tactile contacts with women. || 18 ||

Being composed in meditation, you should entirely avoid all causes of attachment— such as mental preoccupations, the desire for worldly success, and death— as well as women who are objects of enjoyment, and the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest; [instead, remain fixed] on the essence that is the object of the knowledge of Brahman.

Because they are obstacles to the supernatural powers (*siddhis*), some say that those who incite [desire] are to be known as men themselves; for the wise have declared that "mortals who long for enjoyment are called 'women' (kāminīs)," and thus one should abandon association with those who enjoy such things,
just as a man abandons association with a woman— so they explain.
It teaches the knowledge of the discrimination between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), as established in the Sāṃkhya scriptures. || 18 ||
One should not look at a woman who has been violated. || 19 ||

Even though you, the Puruṣa, are not joined with Prakṛti, which consists of the *guṇas*, do not look upon Prakṛti as one who has been robbed [of her power] or as one whose enjoyments have already been experienced by you. The meaning is that you should possess the discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*) that "Prakṛti is one thing and the Puruṣa is another. Alternatively, it means that because you grasp non-difference from Brahman through the intellect, [the world] is essence-less.
It is not even appropriate to seek after proof; for if no distinction is offered, then the very state of being "possessing proof" (siddhimattva) is not a fault—this is the intended meaning. || 19 ||
One should not engage in idle chatter for the sake of dwelling [in the monastery].
Since you have abandoned sport for no other purpose, you should not engage in talk intended merely to display your cleverness; such chatter is a weariness of speech.
One should not contemplate it, for the Śruti declares: "To contemplate forms or words is indeed a weariness of speech. (20)
Do not hold onto anything for the sake of pleasure.
Where there is such a longing for that which generates supramundane bliss, it has been said: "You should not hold onto anything at all.

Or rather, in the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), you should not hold onto anything for the sake of desire for objects; the meaning is that you should remain fixed only upon that object toward which there is no longing. Where...

"Where there is inclination, there is injunction; where there is no [inclination], there is prohibition. This is our discernment, for it has been stated that the scriptures are merely the pulsation of the heart. Also, in the *Vijñānabhairava*:
"Wherever the mind goes, there one should fix [the consciousness]."
Having moved, where will it go? The entire world is composed of Śiva.

Alternatively: "Furthermore, you should not hold onto any collection of objects for the sake of desire; the intended meaning is that one should not follow after passion toward any object whatsoever. And this is to be understood as applying to the stage of one who desires to ascend [to yoga], not to one who has already bathed [in purification]. || 22 ||
One should not be drawn away by sense objects; or rather, you need not perform purification for yourself.

Since [the self] is pure by its very nature due to being of the form of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), there is no requirement for cleansing. As it has been said: "This Lord is eternally pure and beautiful by his own nature; like a temple within a jar or similar object, he does not require washing."
The Lord. || 22 ||
Or you should go to water. || 23 ||

One should not accept even the taste of water that is accompanied by suffering; the word "vā" (or) has the sense of negation. Furthermore, there are three categories: roots (dhātu), prefixes (upasarga), and particles (nipāta).
All words have multiple meanings; their recitation is the illustration of this.
Or alternatively: you should approach—that is, accept as being present before you—the water, which is dull and of the nature of an object, as the class of things to be enjoyed;
you should recognize it as having the form of the enjoyer. Here, the word "or" (vā) serves to exclude the alternative view that consists of sporting with sense objects. || 23 ||
If you were to bathe, you would merely smear the staff with water.
If you were to engage in the enjoyment of sense objects, then you would not be attached to their flavors. || 24 ||
Be shaven-headed, or wear matted locks, or bear the crest-lock. || 25 ||

Since such qualities as yours pertain to the external body, you should not be grasped by means of external signs such as being shaven-headed. If you are liberated in every respect, why should you think, "Shall I be shaven-headed? or "Shall I become one with matted locks? Abandon the concern for external conduct through such reflection.
The essential meaning is: remain outwardly as you please. Or rather, [this refers to] the meaning of the word "vā" (or).

The *muṇḍa*—a synonym for one whose hair has been shorn—is the renouncer of all sense-objects; [the root] *muṇḍi* means "to cut," as in the case of the Pāṇḍavas. The *jaṭila* is the grasper of all sense-objects; [the root] *jaṭa* means "to collect. The *śikhin* is composed of the splendor of knowledge (*jñānatejas*); externally, there is the wearing of a crest-lock (*śikhā*) on the head of the body, while internally, it is the very nature of the flame of knowledge.

It awakens [the practitioner]. Abiding in the domain of the external skull, the external *śikhā* (topknot) has the form of hair and moonbeams; it makes known the true nature (*tattva*) of the internal flame of consciousness, which is denoted by the word *śikhā*. It is the "flame of knowledge that transcends all. Thus.

The external crest-lock (*śikhā*) is likewise merely an indicator of the internal reality (*tattva*). In this same way, it should be understood that the external sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and other such items serve only as indicators. As it has been said:
"This flame of the lamp of knowledge, moving within the space of the heart, having pierced the cavity of the skull..."
It goes upward to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths]. || 25 ||
You should perform the twilight devotions in the evening and in the morning. || 26 ||
When the worldly activity in the form of day has ceased, and when the state of meditative absorption— characterized by the setting of ignorance and appearing as night— has not yet arisen,
there exists in the interval between them a most subtle object of recollection, whose nature is pure consciousness alone.
You should worship the non-union with the self; you should maintain that state of non-union. As it is said in the *Vijñānatantra*:
"When sleep has not yet arrived and the external field of perception has vanished, that supreme Goddess, inaccessible to the mind, shines forth."
And the unification with the supreme reality is also called *saṃdhyā*. || 26 ||
Stand facing the east. || 27 ||

During the morning twilight, when worldly activity is subsiding, you should remain in that twilight characterized by inward-turned awareness; within that state of inwardness, you should exert yourself and apply effort. || 27 ||
Sit facing north. || 28 ||

When the state of emergence gradually arises for the inward-turned yogin, you should remain in that very subsequent twilight which occurs in the interim. The sense is that one should engage in the activity of emergence by relinquishing the state of being inward-turned. || 28 ||
Having uttered "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," you should recite the Sāvitrī mantra beginning with "tatsavitur. || 29 ||
"Oṃ Brahma-bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ; the meaning is: 'All this entire universe is indeed Brahman.

Having spoken thus, and having reflected in this manner, you should recite the Sāvitrī Gāyatrī—the radiant [mantra] pertaining to the Consciousness-Sun (cid-āditya): "We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the Divine; may it impel our intellects."
One should practice this everywhere, at all times, and without interruption;

it has been commenced. It is known as the *Oṃkāra*, renowned everywhere, and experienced by all, belonging to the Sun-like Deity who is the creator of all, whose nature is to sport in the creation of the universe, and who is omnipresent as the maker of everything.

The innate radiance— whose nature is light— is delightful because it is the object of supreme love for Brahman, who is celebrated as the effulgent, most excellent, all-pervading, and omniscient one, and who, as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), impels the intellects of all; this is realized through the meditation on [the Self] as being of the nature of that light.
One should reflect: "Let us cherish the conceit of self-identity with respect to the body and so forth. By this, it is meant that one should contemplate everything as being the Self. || 29 ||
Having gone out before sunset, he should fetch fuel-sticks; one desiring spiritual luster should use *hariṇī* wood. 30.

Desiring the splendor of Brahman (*brahmatejas*), having emerged and arisen from the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) before its cessation, he [the seeker] brings forth the "deer-like" fuel—namely, the non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) of objects. These are the firm arguments (*dṛḍhayukti*) and the knowledges derived from the scriptures (*śāstra*) and other sources that kindle the fire of Brahman; yet, even when such fuel exists, they are not truly useful for the purpose at hand. Thus says the Śruti.
It is heard. || 30 ||
One should perform the recollection at the morning and evening twilights. || 31 ||

"Evening and morning" is an indication of the whole; it refers to the entire day and night. "The practice of the twilight devotions" means constant remembrance. "Going forth completely" means that one must rest in consciousness as something distinct from the body.
If you separate yourself from the body and abide resting in consciousness, then at this very moment you are happy, peaceful, and liberated from bondage.

"Thus you shall become," so says the scripture. And the *saṃdhyā* (the twilight) is the middle between knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*); that which is outside both of them, and which pervades both, is the supreme light. || 31 ||
One must practice the wandering for alms. || 32 ||
One should perform the service of begging for alms morning and evening, and finally, one should carry out the wondrous practice of the instruction on reality.
The kindling of the fire must be performed. || 33 ||
And by that, the kindling of the Brahma-fire should be performed. || 33 ||
You should kindle the fire this very evening. || 34 ||

Thus some say: the enkindling of the Brahma-fire should be performed in the evening, precisely at sunset, according to worldly convention; for if that [sunset] exists, its absence is impossible. Thus say some.
"By not practicing begging," and so forth. || 35 ||
... [she was] one who wandered for alms and tended the sacred fire. || 35 ||
For seven nights. || 36 ||

The two eye-sockets, the two ears, the two nostrils, and the mouth—these are the seven channels. This refers to the evening twilight of the seven channels, so that there may be a non-experience of the enjoyment of objects such as sound; that is, by abandoning the enjoyment of sound and the other sense objects.

As it happens: thus, having not heard [the specific rule], or alternatively, because "seven nights" implies a long duration, one becomes an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow). Therefore, he should perform the vow, which is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). The mere expiation consists of "seven houses," meaning he should beg from many teachers.

Having established association with the virtuous (*sat-saṅga*), proclaiming what has been taught regarding action, and reflecting upon it—since that [knowledge] cannot be obtained from them through mere instruction—he should conduct himself at a single time, having abandoned rising [from meditation]. Remaining solely in a state of composure (*samāhita*), he performs the ritual ablution (*upasparśana*), which is purification; thus, having performed the three daily ablutions throughout day and night, he abides in the characteristics of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Reflecting on the passage beginning with "kāmavakīrṇa" (overwhelmed by desire) and so forth: just as you, though being the Lord, became overwhelmed by desires—that is, distracted by them—by first appearing in the form of an instigator; therefore, because of that instigation, I too have become like that. To You, who are the very longing for longings, I offer my salutation.
The meaning is that whatever you cause me to do out of your own desire leads to my downfall.
He is as if milked by desires; indeed, he is afflicted by desires. He has formed an improper attachment because there is an absence of any impelling force toward those [desires].
The rest is the same: "by the word" means by the cloud, or by meditative absorption (*samādhi*); even in the case of analytical discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), for one who is not indolent.

The cloud of dharma (*dharmamegha*) is always the non-apprehension of distinction (*vivekākhyāti*); this is called "samādhi. By means of samādhi whose characteristics have been established, or else, by means of a long period of time (*abdena*), it becomes pure; thus it is auspicious (*bhadram*).

Oṃ. Whatever object one perceives here through the external sense faculties, that very thing becomes for this person an internal form of dwelling; it transforms into a state of bondage. For a religious student (*brahmacārin*), this applies to speech and the other [senses].
That which is perceivable by the sense faculties of speech and so forth becomes a binder through the lack of the realization: "I am this, I grasp this."
"May it not be so," the teacher prays. || 36 ||
Listen, however, to my words. || 37 ||

And so forth. Because speech is of the nature of the Veda, listen to me. According to the root *uchṛdir*, which signifies "to illuminate" and "to shine," may I illuminate everything through the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of Brahman.
By piercing the darkness of ignorance characterized by the egoistic conceit—"I recite," "I know," "I will," and so forth—[may I illuminate all].
Illuminate that [reality] with the pair of hands; [the syllable] *thak*. The sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is food, which is the nature of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).

Milk (*payas*) is the essence of the *ajapa* [mantra], and it is the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Furthermore, the oblation being offered consists of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and so forth, as well as sound, touch, and the rest. The "flavors" (*rasa*) are those things possessing the quality of being tasted.
And [he is] the form of the power of action consisting of the mental construction of sweet things and so forth. Soma is the nectar that remains from the sacrifice;

it is also the bliss of the sense objects. Sacrifice is the place of worship for the gods; it is the offering of sound and other [objects], and by its casting [into the fire], the satisfaction of the senses. Brahman is characterized by consciousness and bliss; it is accessible through the Vedas. Prajāpati is the creator of the world.

Characterized by a mind intent on Brahman, the religious student, having heard the instruction in the form of the teacher’s words—consisting of blessings and so forth—said everywhere, "Certainly, let it be so. Having bowed to the instruction, he retains it. || 38 ||
Whatever vow belongs to the Vedas, that is the vow here.
The vow (vrata) of the nature to be described hereafter, which is stated in the Veda, constitutes the vow for the religious student (brahmacārī) in this context;
the meaning is that it must necessarily be undertaken. || 39 ||
The Guru said: 40.
"You are a student of sacred knowledge," [he says]. || 40 ||
We shall now follow the sequence of the five modifications. || 41 ||
We shall specifically enumerate the five modifications that are to be performed, beginning with "Thou art a *brahmacārin*. He says this very thing:
"Thou art a *brahmacārin*. [The meaning is: "Being truthful, thou shalt practice—that is, thou shalt know—the *Brahman*, which consists of truth and knowledge. Thus, he is a *brahmacārin*.

Thinking that one who has completed his student life (*anuvrāhma-cārī*) might eat foods with sweet and other tastes, [the author], addressing him as "O knower of Brahman" (*brahmavid*), says: "Are you [such]? || 41 ||
Apośāna || 41 ||
The word "water" (apaḥ) is an elliptical expression for all things beginning with water; thus, the meaning is: "Enjoy the entirety of that which is to be enjoyed.
Now, one might object: "If the mind is seized by objects of enjoyment, how can there be firmness in the contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman? To this, he says: ||| 41 ||
Perform your duty. || 42 ||
The meaning is that it comes about through action (*karman*). In response to the inquiry as to what that action is, he says: || 42 ||
"You slept during the day. || 43 ||

O Conscious Sun (cid-āditya), do not sleep during the day, that is, during the time of illumination; do not be heedless while Brahman, which is all-pervasive, is manifest—even during the state of experiencing objects of enjoyment. One should know the enjoyer to be Brahman, whose nature consists of both the tasted and the taster. This is the intended meaning.

The sense is that Brahman—which is self-luminous, possesses its own form, and is established within itself—cannot be the object of denial; for apart from that [Brahman], they themselves would be diminished. Thus, warding off concern for objects, he instructs [the disciple]. 43.
And he who [speaks] speech. || 44 ||

The meaning is: having restrained speech, make your speech characterized by the Middle Path and peaceful; having abandoned discursive thought (*vikalpa*) and established the discernment of consciousness (*cid-vimarśa*) within the mind, enjoy everything without attachment.
He says this to cause one to abandon association with the ignorant, which brings about thoughts of objects of enjoyment. || 44 ||
Do not look upon me wearing soiled garments. || 45 ||

Impurity (*mala*) is threefold: the sense of incompleteness (*apūrṇamanyatā*), which is the impurity of limited agency (*āṇava*); the impurity of objective manifestation (*māyīya*), consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the pleasant and unpleasant within the differentiated world; and the impurity of desire (*kāma*). Impurity is that which possesses an obscuration (*upādhi*) by its very nature; such is the obscuration of the latent impressions. *Māyā* is a synonym for the world (*jagad-aṇḍa*).
You should not look upon these who are clothed in soiled garments. || 45 ||
You should speak for a month. || 46 ||
Therefore, even conversation with them is improper.

This is because attachment gives rise to delusion. The meaning is that for those who have cast off the garments of worldly objects, who possess the reflective awareness of pure awakening, and who perceive the world as having the singular nature of Brahman—devoid of limiting adjuncts such as genus and form—attachment must be abandoned. As it has been said: "Attachment must be renounced in every respect."
If it is not possible to abandon attachment entirely, then one should certainly avoid the fault of association with those who are harmful to Śiva. And so it is said:
Those wearing soiled garments, women in their courses, women who have recently given birth, those who are impure, and the Antyāvasāyins—these are [the ones referred to]. || 47 ||
Women who are *udakyā* (menstruating), those in their courses, women who have recently given birth and for whom the ten-day period has not yet passed,

dog-cookers (*śvapāka*), women associated with *yukkasas*, those who are impure, those deficient in the purity required by the duties of their respective stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*), and the lowest castes (*antyāvasāyin*) such as *caṇḍālas*— and indeed, whoever else is unworthy of association, of these [one must avoid].

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all [such persons]. [The phrase] "those such as a woman in her courses" (*udakyādyāḥ*) means they do not become [excluded]; rather, it is only those with soiled garments (*malavadvāsasaḥ*) who are [excluded]. The logical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Those such as a woman in her courses do not become [excluded]. Since every sentence is restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇam*), the word "only" (*eva*) is used for this very reason.

One should go [to him]. Even if they were women clad in pure white garments or even those in their courses (udakyā), contact with them would not be defiling at all. As it is said in the Vaiṣṇava scripture:
"O Lord whose navel is the lotus, from one endowed with the six qualities, [one attains purity] within twenty-six [days]."
One who turns away from the lotus-feet of Śūlapāṇi, the most excellent of gods,
and instead offers his mind, speech, and life for the sake of worldly benefit, does not purify his own lineage; indeed, such a person possesses great pride.

Just as one avoids a woman in her courses and the like in public because such contact causes sin, so too a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should abandon attachment to ignorance; this is the intended meaning. 47.
One should not go to a cremation ground. || 48 ||
Because it is a mass of bones, flesh, and so forth, one should not go toward the body in the cremation ground. The meaning is that one should abandon the conceit, "This is my body. || 48 ||
You shall not see a corpse. 49.
The entire world, characterized by body after body, is seen as nothing more than the physical body because its limbs and members are woven together with consciousness (*cit*).

One would not truly know it [as such] if one were to perceive it merely as a body, for that body exists only in the absence of [the realization of] that [consciousness]; it is, in reality, pure consciousness alone. This is not so, however, for one whose true nature as the Self has been forgotten through ignorance (*avidyā*), who fails to know it [in this way].
Anticipating the question "What should be done?", he says: || 49 ||
If you see a corpse that has not been covered with grass, you should fast for three nights. || 40 ||
"Without grass" means uncovered; "with the vision of pure consciousness alone" means with the state of objective phenomena dispelled.

Having looked upon your own body as if it were a corpse and having seen the world [in that same way], you should fast for three nights—for a long time—so that there is no manifestation of the triad of knower, knowledge, and the known, or in such a manner that this occurs.
Even if you practice fasting, it will not bring about the unification of all the senses through the cessation of mental fluctuations;
rather, you should cultivate a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by the absence of contact with external objects, so that ignorance may never touch you again. (40)
Having consumed honey or meat, or having caused injury to the body, you must undertake the vow again. || 41 ||

Regarding "honey and meat" as indicative of all objects of enjoyment— or, in relation to the preceding context, regarding "the month of honey" (Caitra)— one who eats every object of enjoyment while touching the body, that is, grasping the physical frame and identifying with it, [is called a consumer]. Again, the vow is characterized by renunciation, which is abiding in one's own pure essential nature.

You should take [them]. By the consumption of honey and meat, the act of eating is characterized by the enjoyment of objects of pleasure that provide satisfaction; if an immersion in such enjoyments occurs, then, having touched and killed the body, one must again maintain the state of being established in the vow.

"You should perform [this]. The root *labh* preceded by the prefix *ā-* has the sense of killing. Here, "laying hold of the body" (*dehālaṃbhanam*) means only the reviling of the body, not its actual slaughter. For what reason does this obsession with being enjoyed by the *rasika* (one who relishes aesthetic flavor) arise in me? To answer "why," he says: || 51 ||
Whatever things are defilements of the sacrificial offering, those are [defilements] of the food. 52.
Those things which have not been offered into the self as an oblation into the fire—there is a fault in eating them, for by such eating one falls from one's state.
The meaning is that one should eat only after all activities have been offered into the self. 52.
You should not eat the leavings of another. || 53 ||
In this context, "remnants" (ucchiṣṭa) refers to the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth, because pleasure is enjoyed by all. To enjoy those [objects] is what causes one to fall. 53.
One should not give the leavings of food to another. || 54 ||

Even the pleasure of the sense-objects is enjoyed as something residual; if you were to offer that [residue] to Him, then you would not be eating it. Rather, having offered it to the Consciousness-Self alone, you should eat it with detachment through firm resolve.
Surely, if this has been experienced by the Gurus, then even innate pleasure is not residual. And therefore—
Anticipating the question of how it is to be experienced, he says: || 54 ||
Indeed, the teachers say that one may eat the remains of what has been tasted by one's guru at will. || 55 ||

The phrase "hyarthe" means that there is nothing to be done by one regarding the experience of the ultimate supreme bliss already experienced by the gurus; for this is the meaning of the guru’s instruction. By this, he prohibits the excessive indulgence in enjoyment that might otherwise arise due to the absence of non-attachment toward such enjoyment. || 55 ||
Do not eat heavy food. || 56 ||

For the sake of maintaining the elements and the vital breaths, which are the means for the non-destruction of consciousness, one should consume some food; however, the rule does not apply when there is an excess of enjoyment. This is because of the statement: "One should take food for the sake of maintaining the vital breaths. (56)
This refers to the case of one who is ill. || 57 ||

The meaning of this statement prohibiting the enjoyment of heavy food is that one who is afflicted by disease is the subject here. This prohibition applies to one for whom the enjoyment of heavy food results in a specific mental distress (*ādhi*) in the form of attachment;

it does not mean, however, that there is either a rule or a prohibition regarding enjoyment for one who is unattached—this is the intended sense. [Objection: But what about occasional worldly existence?

If there should arise an attachment to sense objects for one who is immersed in the flavor of those objects, whose self has been forgotten, and who is being whirled here and there by the wind like a tuft of cotton— then, in response to the inquiry as to what means there might be for its removal, he says: || 57 ||
By whatever means he may be cured. || 58 ||

By that very rule of the independent Lord (Svatantra-Īśvara) through which one becomes intent on cutting [the bonds], by that same means one should perform the treatment. This is the intended meaning: you must remain single-mindedly devoted to the Lord. Just as the Lord causes one to grasp at false objects, so too, having established the mind upon the Praṇava—the ultimate innate bliss—he [withdraws it] from the sense objects.

And no inherent calamity will ever cause it to turn back; rather, you must bring about its cessation through the worship of the Lord. Alternatively, one should not treat the mind with medicine by suppressing desire for whatever object and by whatever means;
instead, one should divert the child-like mind by granting that very enjoyment in measured doses. Otherwise, it may reach the extreme limit [of agitation].

The meaning is that the mind's ascent toward sense objects occurs. Even through the complete renunciation of sense objects, the mind runs toward them object by object. Whether through lack of desire or through enjoyment obtained by chance, the mind inevitably descends from sense objects; this is simply the inherent nature of the mind. As it has been said:
"If one does not perceive [the truth], it is said that even by means of renunciation, one merely ascends to higher objects; therefore, one should abandon even those. (58)
But was it not said: "You should eat"? (59)

Having kindled the fire of discrimination regarding the objects of the senses, you should eat as if having already offered them into it with a focused mind, making the light of consciousness manifest in everything through the contemplation of the all-pervading nature of Consciousness (*cinmaya*). Even while in the state of worldly activity (*vyutthāna*),
remaining inward-turned by virtue of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of samādhi, you should enjoy the object of experience like one who is intoxicated, yet not [as a slave to it].
The meaning is: "again, by means of the cultivation of enjoyment. || 59 ||
One should not eat from an earthenware vessel.

The locative case in "mṛṇmaye dehe" (in the earthen body) indicates the cause; the meaning is that you should enjoy those objects such as sound and so forth which serve for the nourishment of the body, yet you should practice the renunciation of sense-objects. || 60 ||
Some say that one should not reconnect [the lineage]. 61.
One should not practice renunciation that is contrary to the reconnection [of the self],
for some eminent teachers have said that even when objects are enjoyed without attachment, they do not become defiling. || 61 ||
Standing and sitting. || 62 ||

That in which one stands—that is, the body—is the *sthāna* (place); that is the *āsana* (seat). Its abandonment means the relinquishing of identification with the body (*dehābhimāna*). Alternatively, *sthāna* is the sun (*savitṛ*), for by it one stands; in that regard, *āsana* means being subject to one-pointedness (*ekatānatā*). [The root] *ās* is used in the sense of sitting. 62.
In the preceding sections, fasting and the restraint of speech were prescribed.

When that which was previously described—the seventh [state] of the existent—and the cessation of speech (vāntha) occur, then there shall be the destruction of the knots, the bonds, and the intoxications such as desire, anger, and so forth, within the range of the objects of consciousness;
the plural number is used because of the multiplicity of these related factors. (63)
Having seen even a small amount of fire, one is purified by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
If one sees something that is even slightly impure, unpeaceful, or unpleasant—
whether it be an unpleasant sight or something that may be beneficial or harmful to oneself— and having seen it with attachment,
one becomes impure through being affected by it, one becomes purified by performing breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). And as for breath-control:

The restraint (*āyāma*) of the vital breaths— which constitute the living being, as well as all objects of affection such as garlands and other things— is the cessation of the mind's fluctuations through the absence of objective referents by means of the contemplation of Brahman (*brahmabhāvanā*) everywhere.

The synonyms for *samādhi* are expressed in the plural to indicate that for one whose mind has been carried away by sense objects, there must be a repeated application toward the state of oneness with Brahman; this is stated because of the address "O son of Kuntī" [in the Gītā] regarding practice (*abhyāsa*). Alternatively, it refers to the vitalizing of the life-force and the seeing of the eye, according to the Śruti: "The life-force of the life-force, the eye of the eye. It also signifies the prolongation of the entire living being.

Having dissolved away all contraction within the entire range of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), there is nothing other than the very state of being inlaid with the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). The "lengthening" of the breath—which belongs to every living being and is the Supreme Lord—by means of those [breaths], is purification;
that is to say, purification occurs solely through the abundance of the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cidvimarśa*). || 64 ||
In the case of a formal presentation, three [steps] are to be performed. || 65 ||
The number "three" is used for measurement because even a slight stain is purified by merely seeing [the sun] for three moments. || 65 ||
Then, having uttered [the words], there are seven.

The word "seven" is an illustration by way of inclusion of many more. Now, immediately after seeing [the deity], when there is utterance—consisting of those words externally and characterized by reflection internally—the seven tasks are to be performed.
Furthermore, because one reflects upon that immediately after seeing [the deity], impurity increases excessively through such attachment.
Through great effort for the sake of purification, the mind—even when it has gone toward sense objects—must be drawn back again by means of the singular focus on Brahman. 66.
But in the case of compounds, there are twelve. || 67 ||

"Twelve" is an indication of even more [than that]. The word "atho" (then/therefore) also connects here. Having encountered death immediately after seeing [the deity], one whose mind is fixed upon that object should perform the twelvefold rite; for one who is excessively defiled, purification must be performed again and again with great effort and exceeding exertion.
One should practice with a concentrated mind. Anticipating the question of how one becomes pure by means of this, he says: || 67 ||
Everywhere there is the sight of light and the touching of water. 68.

The meaning is that in every case of purification, the very sight of light—that is, illumination—is the cause of purification, serving as the ritual sipping of water (*udakopasparśana*). However, in response to the inquiry "What is the light?", he says: || 68 ||
"The sun and the moon, fire, and the Brāhmaṇa—by even one of these she becomes pure. (69)
Regarding these five luminaries, beginning with the sun:
their essential nature is that single light which is the very form of the Self (ātman), attained through the relinquishing of the notion of forms.

Although it exists as a single light, it appears as if divided into distinct forms such as the sun and so forth due to the influence of sound and other factors. [This refers to] the forms of the sun and the rest.

Because it is superimposed upon that [Light], it lacks existence apart from the nature of that [Light]; thus, through the removal of its cultivation, when that very Supreme Light— the Self in the form of consciousness— is seen and experienced as one's own self, it is purified, casting off the impurity of limiting adjuncts such as birth and form.

And for the very purpose of seeing that [Brahman], the practice of *prāṇāyāma*—which is synonymous with the withdrawal of the senses (*viṣayapratyahāra*) and consists in the state of oneness with Brahman—is taught. Having heard this instruction, the religious student (*brahmacārī*), having accomplished much effort and seeking the knowledge of Brahman, takes refuge in initiation (*dīkṣā*) alone. || 69 ||
"Shake off the poverty of the mind; the eye is the sun, the best of lights. O consecration, do not harm me!"—with these words, one should gaze at the sun by day and at the fire by night.

Shake off the fickle mind; it does not become firmly established in the one Brahman. The eye, though it perceives objects, does not reach a state of desirelessness even when impoverished by them; therefore, the mind becomes attached to the objects brought before it. And that which is the sun, the conscious light, the purifier, the best among all luminaries—[it is this that must be sought].

The unsurpassed light cannot be grasped by the external sun and so forth during the day, nor can it be apprehended by a mind bound by worldly attachments, nor even by the eye of the destitute. || 70 ||
"Initiate me; do not harm me," [he said]. || 71 ||

Because of the shift in word order in the phrase "the sun by day and fire by night," [it means]: O Initiation, I take refuge in you alone. You alone are that which consists of the teachings already spoken and those yet to be spoken. Forgetfulness is the *māyā* of darkness (*tāmasī*).
Like the sun by day and like fire by night, you are self-luminous; you illuminate everything, both night and day.
Brahman. || 71 ||
Do not harm me! || 72 ||
Because its true nature has been forgotten, it seems to attain the state of becoming everything everywhere. Do not act [in this way].

Whenever even my own essential nature (*svātmarūpa*) might seem to have been forgotten through the grasping of objects such as Brahman, at that very moment, having come here and removed those objects by means of the contemplation of Brahman (*brahmabhāvanā*) everywhere—

The intention is that one should contemplate the radiance of Brahman. Seeing [the disciple] as if distressed by the possibility of forgetting even the supreme, all-pervading splendor, [the teacher] instructs him in the means for its removal. || 72 ||
When semen is emitted, one should mutter: "May my faculty return to me. (73)

When the semen—which is the form of all power and consists of the succession of one's own self and the other—has been emitted and there is forgetfulness, one should reflect thus: "May my organ return to me. (73)

May this sense-organ come back to me; may life return, may fortune return, may sacred knowledge return to me, and may wealth return to me. Whatever seed of mine has fallen upon the earth, whatever has flowed away into the water, whatever seed of mine is spilled—may it be gathered back.
Whatever is born from me again, or whatever shall be established within me—by that, make me immortal; by that, make me possessed of good offspring. 74.

Even when one has died during the state of meditative absorption (samādhi), the sense-faculties—such as the eye and so forth—may come to me or depart from me. For there is no harm whatsoever to me, since those faculties do not actually arrive, being unreal by virtue of being superimposed [upon consciousness]. Furthermore, what kind of sense-faculty is it? The word "punaḥ" is used in the sense of "again and again," indicating multiplicity.
Possessing great vital energy (*vahvāyu*), it exists for a long time within meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in a conceptualized form;

furthermore, what kind of portion is it? It possesses great sovereignty (*bahvaiśvarya*), capable of grasping various objects of perception—the change in gender is according to Vedic usage—and it is the Brahman hidden within the sense-objects.

May the knowledge of Brahman come to me; may wealth again enter my heart; may that which is the form of supreme splendor come to me. The sense is: "Whether in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or upon rising from it, there shall be no loss for me, who am established equally everywhere. That seed of mine which has fallen upon the earth—
The root *skand* is used in the senses of moving and drying; it is an archaic (chāndasa) verb.

That which is my semen—consciousness (*cit*), form, and power—which has gone to the earth, having become of the nature of the earth, and which has flowed over the plants; and that which has gone into the waters—and which, though manifold in form, [remains] even so.

I alone have brought this to completion. That [creation] does not transcend my own nature, nor has it become something other than me, such that I might forget myself. My own innate form—the semen, which is consciousness in its entirety and manifoldness—is poured forth; it becomes as if sprinkled upon the objects of the senses. That which is born from me spreads everywhere.
It becomes manifest once again. And that which abides in me—surely even the objects of the senses abide therein.
It exists as if it were the Imperishable (Acyuta). By means of that consciousness, make me immortal.
For Death himself fears that consciousness, which is the *praṇava* within the mind; and by means of that, may I have excellent offspring.

The desire for the continuity of progeny arises, characterized by knowledge and action; [therefore,] "make that [progeny] beautiful, beneficial, and never forsaking those like myself"—this is the prayer to the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*), which burns the fuel of all sins. Through this contemplation, the Lord sports within the universe like a sovereign monarch.
Śiva is auspicious, for he causes everything—including the enemy of poverty and all that is feared by his adversaries—to shine. || 74 ||
Now follows the instruction on the vow of the Four Hotṛ-priests (Cāturhotṛka).

Now, one might object: "If the four—Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, characterized as consciousness, mind, intellect, and ego—are indeed the four officiating priests (cāturhotṛka) in the ritual of the entire universe, and if the Hotṛ priests are to be meditated upon as such, then does this not result in duality? To this he replies, "No. (75)
You should not sit with four; you should not eat in the presence of four; you should not sit with four. 76.

Regarding those [objects], you should not remain as if having entered into attachment to them by perceiving them through the intellect (*buddhi*). Or, let there be the perception of them; yet, wherever their presence may be, you should plant the seed [of awareness] there, transformed by you into their very form—namely, the objects themselves.
By transcending that [perception], one should exist. Because of the transformation into that very form, you should therefore not remain together with them.

Having worshipped those [four *caturhotṛ* sacrifices], you should consume even that as the Absolute (*tattva*). However, you should consume every object of enjoyment solely through the contemplation of Brahman (*brahmabhāvanā*), because there is no distinction between those four and the nature of Brahman.
For the Śruti states regarding the *caturhotṛ* rites: "Brahman indeed is the four *hotṛ*s. Thus, their status as objects of worship is declared.
This is for the purpose of teaching that [the world] is non-different from consciousness. He clarifies this very point: || 76 ||
Or you may eat alone. || 77 ||

"Abiding as Brahman alone, you should enjoy; becoming Brahman itself through the knowledge of Brahman, perform all actions"—thus [ends the teaching of] Śiva. Here, although there is an explanation by Ācāryātreya regarding the manifest external object which must necessarily be accepted by those of the three twice-born classes:

The disclosure of internal meaning by means of the *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and *abalā* plants is called "obstruction" (*ruddhi*). This occurs specifically in the first stage (*āśrama*) for the purpose of generating the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). If, during the very state of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), one who has received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) should become established in discernment, dispassion, and so forth, then—what [further need would there be]?

"Since it is heard in the Śruti: 'One should renounce on that very day on which one becomes dispassionate through weariness with the support of the stages of life (āśramas),' therefore the gurus should forgive him for setting out upon this exceedingly profound path of action. (79)
Oṃ! Bhairava is indeed one, without a second, manifesting in manifold forms;
he is united with the state that extends from the single Śivā down to the totality of all things. || 1 ||
Thus, this entire path, possessing a state of non-difference from Bhairava,
appears as if attaining independence through His own sovereignty.
Abiding in the nature of the Mother (Mātṛkā), this is divided as the path of mantra;
by virtue of its nature as valid cognition (pramā), it is likewise called the path of phonemes (varṇa).
Having attained the nature of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), this [object] proceeds to the state of being a word-meaning (padārtha);
yet, without abandoning its immersion in the nature of the means of valid cognition, it attains the state of being an object of knowledge (meyatā).
Because it proceeds through association with the worlds, the path of the parts (kalādhvan) is conjoined with the Mothers;
when there is conjunction with pure objectivity, let it be understood as the path of the principles (tattvādhvan).
Due to its association with being the substratum for that [grossness], it is described as the "path of the worlds" (bhuvana-adhvan).
It is based solely on the portion of the subject consisting of innate bliss;
however, when resting in mere emptiness, the state becomes one whose nature is devoid of bliss. || 1 ||

When the state of being an object of knowledge comes to rest, supreme bliss fully arises; for when the entire mass of infinite objects of knowledge is completely filled by the object of knowledge on all sides, [that bliss is attained]. || 2 ||
Through the union with the relish [of consciousness] arising from the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), there is the state known as "Great Bliss" (mahānanda).
For the Knower who devours all, both the subject and all objects of knowledge are but a mental construction.
When it attains a rest that is free from limiting adjuncts and self-sufficient, then indeed there is the bliss of consciousness, unenhanced by anything insentient.
And therein there is no fixed abode whatsoever, differentiated in the form of the *iḍā*;
where there is no exclusion of anything, that [reality] vibrates everywhere as the universe.
That which is unstruck consciousness, conjoined with the supreme nectar—
that very abode of universal bliss our Guru has proclaimed.
Thus [ends] the venerable *Abhinavagupta*’s commentary on the *Mālinīvijayottara*.
Likewise, in that very same [text]:
"Therefore, that power of unfolding which was previously non-differentiated,
and which consists of the nature of the unfolding of objective existence— that is the state of Puruṣa."
That which is non-different is ungraspable, and that which is the Lord is the non-grasper;
now, they know that which is established as the graspable to be the grasper by virtue of its excellence.
Since it is proclaimed as being called "Puruṣa" due to its connection with the commencement of creation,
and because of its clear self-recognition, it is also termed "Mukhavaktra."
Even though differentiation has arisen, it undergoes contraction within that very [consciousness] alone, by virtue of which those two—
the enjoyer and the enjoyed— become indistinctly merged.
In this state, that entire universe appears as if unborn;
therefore, the *sadyojāta* plane is empty and devoid of the nature of sensation.
Therefore, in this Sadyojāta state, the primary condition is considered to be Aghora;
and although that [condition] consists of contraction, it will result in the expansion of consciousness.
Because Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa are dissolved therein, it forcibly casts them below;
beginning with "consisting of the nature of reality" (vastubhāvamayī), such is the state whose presiding deities are the ten Rudras.
Therefore, the universe— situated above and discerned by the radiance of the weight of awakening—
is desired to be assimilated into the conscious self by those whose lives are animated by consciousness.
Because he possesses the power of self-awareness as a latent impression, the Lord is called Vāma; may there be auspiciousness.
Oṃ. Sons fathered by men upon women of the same class as themselves are designated by the names of the social orders (varṇas) and are known as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. || 1 ||
Sons who are begotten by men of the highest caste upon women of lower castes are indeed of six kinds; these are the *anuloma* (born in the natural order).
Those sons who are begotten by men of lower caste upon women of higher caste are of six kinds; these are known as those born in the inverse order (pratiloma).
From other men, women—whether their husband is dead or living—beget sons; know these to be of two kinds, born of adultery (jāraja).
The castes (varṇas) are said to be exactly four, while the sub-castes (upavarṇas) are fourteen;
six are declared to be born in the natural order (anuloma), and those born in the reverse order (pratiloma) are equal in number to them.
Two more are said to be born of adultery; thus, there are eighteen castes.
Furthermore, if those of similar status produce offspring with women of lower castes, [the following result].
From those sons born of them, various sub-castes (upavarṇakas) are indeed produced;
otherwise, due to the confusion of castes, the Mleccha tribes are born.
Those born from men of the highest Mleccha castes by women of lower castes are proclaimed as Pratilomas; those remaining after them are likewise Pratilomas, and from them also are born the Anulomas.
Those of lower castes are more refined than them, and among them, the Brāhmaṇa is superior;
he is the teacher and worshipful one for all, as he reveals that Brahman within each and every being.
[Thus ends the determination of the eighteen classes.]
